topic: Earth in the Solar System & Its Motions

items.title: The Solar System — Origin, Members & Planets
items.body:
### The Solar System — Origin and Members

**In one line**
The solar system is the Sun plus everything held by its gravity — eight planets and smaller bodies — all formed from one cloud of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago.

**The story**
Long ago a vast cloud of gas and dust (a **nebula**) began to collapse under its own gravity. Most of it — about 99.9% — fell to the centre, grew hot and became the **Sun**. The leftover material spread into a flat spinning disc, and inside it tiny grains stuck together, grew into pebbles, then boulders, then whole **planets** — a slow sticking process called **accretion**. This picture is the **Nebular Hypothesis** of Kant and Laplace. The planets split into two families: four small rocky **terrestrial** worlds near the Sun, and four large gassy **Jovian** giants farther out, with a belt of asteroids between them.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Prelims loves the Kant–Laplace name, the 4.6-billion-year age, and the terrestrial-versus-Jovian split.

**Picture it**

| Group | Planets | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Terrestrial (inner) | Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | small, rocky, dense, few moons |
| Jovian (outer) | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune | large, gaseous, many moons |

Beyond Neptune lies the icy **Kuiper Belt** (30–50 AU, home to Pluto) and, far out, the **Oort Cloud**, the source of long-period comets.

**Terms explained**
- **Nebula** — a cloud of gas and dust in space.
- **Accretion** — the sticking-together of small particles to build larger bodies.
- **AU (Astronomical Unit)** — the Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km.

**The small bodies — where they sit**

| Region / body | What it is |
|---|---|
| Asteroid Belt | a rocky-metallic leftover (remnant) zone between Mars and Jupiter |
| Ceres | the largest asteroid in that belt — now classed as a dwarf planet |
| Kuiper Belt | a belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune (30–50 AU), home to Pluto |
| Oort Cloud | a distant spherical shell of icy bodies — the source of long-period comets |

**Don't confuse**
Terrestrial planets are the small rocky inner four; Jovian are the big gassy outer four. The asteroid belt sits between Mars and Jupiter, not beyond Neptune.

**Remember it**
"One cloud, 4.6 billion years ago: Sun takes 99.9%, the scraps make the planets."

**TL;DR**
- Solar system = Sun + 8 planets + dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
- Nebular Hypothesis (Kant–Laplace); formed about 4.6 billion years ago; Sun holds about 99.9% of the matter.
- Inner four rocky (terrestrial), outer four gaseous (Jovian); asteroid belt between.
- Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune; Oort Cloud is the comet source; 1 AU is about 150 million km.
keyPoints: Solar system = Sun + 8 planets + dwarf planets + moons + asteroids + comets + meteoroids.
Nebular Hypothesis (Kant–Laplace): Sun took ~99.9% of the collapsing nebula's matter, formed ~4.6 billion years ago.
Terrestrial (inner) planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — small, rocky, dense.
Jovian (outer) planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — large, gaseous; Uranus & Neptune are ice giants.
Asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter; Kuiper Belt (30–50 AU) beyond Neptune; Oort Cloud is the comet source.
1 Astronomical Unit (AU) ≈ 150 million km.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Stars and The Solar System

items.title: Distinctive Planet & Small-Body Facts
items.body:
### Distinctive Planet and Small-Body Facts

**In one line**
Each planet has one or two "odd-one-out" facts that examiners test, and the small bodies (dwarf planets, comets, meteorites) have their own clear definitions.

**The story**
Going out from the Sun: **Mercury** is the smallest and closest, with a huge day-to-night temperature swing. **Venus** is the show-stopper — the **hottest** planet (a runaway greenhouse of carbon dioxide), it spins backwards (**retrograde**), and its day (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 days). **Mars** is the rusty **Red Planet**. **Jupiter** is the largest, and its moon **Ganymede** is the biggest moon in the whole solar system. **Saturn** has its famous rings and the moon **Titan**. **Uranus** rolls on its side, and **Neptune** has the **fastest winds** (about 2,100 km/h). Smaller bodies follow their own rules, explained below.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
"Which planet is hottest / largest / windiest / spins backwards" is a guaranteed single-fact question.

**Picture it**

| Planet | The fact to remember |
|---|---|
| Mercury | smallest, closest, biggest day–night temperature range |
| Venus | hottest, retrograde, day longer than year |
| Mars | Red Planet (iron oxide) |
| Jupiter | largest; moon Ganymede is the biggest moon |
| Neptune | fastest winds (~2,100 km/h) |
| Uranus | axis tipped almost into its orbit |

**Beyond the solar system — four terms**

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| Milky Way | the barred-spiral galaxy that contains the solar system |
| Andromeda | the nearest large (major) galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away |
| Light-year | the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km — a unit of distance, not time |
| Proxima Centauri | the nearest star to the Sun, about 4.24 light-years away |

**Terms explained**
- **Retrograde** — spinning in the opposite direction to most planets.
- **Dwarf planet** — orbits the Sun and is round but has **not cleared** its orbital path (Pluto, Eris, Ceres).
- **Meteoroid → meteor → meteorite** — a rock in space, then the streak of light as it burns, then the piece that reaches the ground.

**Don't confuse**
Venus is the hottest planet, not Mercury (even though Mercury is closer) — Venus's thick carbon-dioxide blanket traps the heat. A meteor is the flash; a meteorite is what lands.

**Remember it**
"Venus: hottest, backwards, lazy (day longer than year). Neptune: windiest. Jupiter: biggest, with the biggest moon."

**TL;DR**
- Venus: hottest, retrograde, day longer than year.
- Mercury smallest and closest; Mars is the Red Planet.
- Jupiter largest; its moon Ganymede is the biggest moon of all.
- Dwarf planet fails only the "cleared its orbit" test; meteoroid → meteor → meteorite.
keyPoints: Venus: hottest planet, retrograde spin, day longer than year, densest terrestrial atmosphere.
Mercury: smallest, closest to Sun, greatest day–night temperature range.
Jupiter largest; Ganymede (its moon) is the biggest moon in the solar system, larger than Mercury.
Neptune has the fastest planetary winds (~2,100 km/h); Uranus's axis lies almost in its orbital plane.
Dwarf planet fails only the 'cleared its orbit' criterion — e.g. Pluto, Eris, Ceres.
Meteoroid → meteor (shooting star) → meteorite (reaches surface); comets have highly elliptical orbits.

items.title: The Sun, the Moon & Eclipses
items.body:
### The Sun, the Moon and Eclipses

**In one line**
The Sun is a ball of hydrogen and helium that powers the system by fusion; the Moon only reflects its light; and eclipses happen when Sun, Earth and Moon line up.

**The story**
The **Sun** is mostly **hydrogen (about 75%)** and **helium (about 24%)**, and holds about **99.86%** of all the mass in the solar system. Deep in its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, releasing the energy that reaches us as sunlight after an **8 minute 20 second** journey. Dark patches called **sunspots** are simply *cooler* areas of its surface. The **Moon** makes no light of its own — it reflects the Sun's, and as it circles the Earth we see its lit portion change through **phases** over about **29 days**. When the three bodies line up, we get an **eclipse**: Earth's shadow on the Moon (a **lunar** eclipse) or the Moon's shadow on the Earth (a **solar** eclipse).

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
"Sunspots hotter or cooler", the Sun's composition, and the new-moon/full-moon eclipse rule are repeat questions.

**Picture it**

| Eclipse | Who is in the middle | Moon phase |
|---|---|---|
| Lunar | Earth, between Sun and Moon | Full Moon |
| Solar | Moon, between Sun and Earth | New Moon |

**Terms explained**
- **Fusion** — joining light atoms into heavier ones, releasing energy.
- **Umbra / penumbra / antumbra** — the full shadow (total), the partial shadow (partial), and the shadow beyond the umbra's tip (annular "ring of fire").
- **Saros cycle** — the roughly 18-year-11-day gap after which a similar eclipse repeats.

**Don't confuse**
A lunar eclipse happens only on a Full Moon, a solar eclipse only on a New Moon. Sunspots are cooler (darker), not hotter.

**Remember it**
"Solar eclipse = New Moon; Lunar eclipse = fuLL Moon."

**TL;DR**
- Sun: about 75% hydrogen, 24% helium; about 99.86% of the system's mass; light reaches us in 8 min 20 s.
- Sunspots are cooler, darker patches; the Sun's energy comes from core fusion.
- The Moon reflects sunlight; its phases repeat about every 29 days.
- Lunar eclipse on a Full Moon; solar eclipse on a New Moon; shadow terms umbra, penumbra, antumbra.
keyPoints: Sun: ~75% hydrogen, ~24% helium; ~99.86% of the solar system's mass; sunlight reaches Earth in 8 min 20 s.
Sunspots are cooler (darker) patches on the photosphere; energy = core nuclear fusion.
Moon reflects sunlight; phases repeat ~every 29 days; formed by a giant impact ('big splat').
Lunar eclipse: Earth between Sun and Moon, only on a Full Moon; Solar eclipse: Moon between Sun and Earth, only on a New Moon.
Umbra = total, penumbra = partial, antumbra = annular 'ring of fire'.
Saros cycle ≈ 18 years 11 days for eclipse repetition.

items.title: Earth's Motions — Rotation, Revolution & Seasons
items.body:
### Earth's Motions — Rotation, Revolution and Seasons

**In one line**
The Earth both spins (rotation, giving day and night) and orbits the Sun (revolution), and because its axis stays tilted, that orbit gives us the seasons.

**The story**
The Earth **rotates** from west to east on its axis once in about **24 hours**, so one side faces the Sun (day) while the other is dark (night). Its axis is not upright — it leans, sitting at **66½° to the orbital plane**, which is the same as a **23½° tilt from the vertical**. Meanwhile the Earth **revolves** around the Sun once in **365¼ days** along an oval (elliptical) path. The spare quarter-day each year is saved up and added as one extra day every four years — a **leap year**. The seasons come from the tilt: as the Earth travels round, first the Northern and then the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, so the overhead sun shifts between the two tropics.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The 66½°/23½° equivalence, the leap-year reason, and the solstice/equinox dates are all high-frequency facts.

**Picture it**

| Event | Date | Sun overhead | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Summer solstice | 21 June | Tropic of Cancer | longest Northern day; midnight sun at Arctic Circle |
| Winter solstice | 22 December | Tropic of Capricorn | longest Southern day |
| Equinoxes | 21 Mar and 23 Sep | Equator | day equals night everywhere |

**The Coriolis effect (Ferrel's Law)**
Because the Earth spins, anything moving freely over it — winds, ocean currents, aircraft — is turned aside. In the **Northern Hemisphere it is deflected to its right**, in the **Southern Hemisphere to its left**. The deflecting force is **zero at the Equator and increases towards the poles**. It matters for large, long-distance movements such as planetary winds and ocean currents, and is negligible for slow, short ones. It is why cyclones spin anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern.

**Terms explained**
- **Rotation** — the daily spin on the axis.
- **Revolution** — the yearly orbit around the Sun.
- **Circle of illumination** — the line dividing the lit (day) half from the dark (night) half.
- **Perihelion / aphelion** — the nearest point (about January) and farthest point (about July) of Earth's orbit.

**Two everyday results of the spin**
- Because the Earth rotates **from west to east**, the Sun appears to **rise in the east and set in the west**.
- All places on the **same meridian** have the **same local (sun) time**, because they face the Sun at the same moment.

**Don't confuse**
Rotation gives day and night; revolution (with the tilt) gives the seasons. The 66½° is measured to the orbital *plane*, which is the same as 23½° from the vertical.

**Remember it**
"Spin = day; orbit + tilt = seasons. 66½° to the plane means 23½° off upright."

**TL;DR**
- Rotation: west to east, about 24 hours, axis tilted 23½° from vertical, causing day/night and the Coriolis effect.
- Revolution: oval orbit in 365¼ days, giving a leap year every four years.
- Solstices 21 Jun (Cancer) and 22 Dec (Capricorn); equinoxes 21 Mar and 23 Sep (Equator).
- The poles get about six months of day then six months of night.
keyPoints: Rotation: west→east, ~24 h, axis tilted 66½° to orbital plane (23½° from vertical) → day/night + Coriolis effect.
Circle of illumination (day–night line) does not align with the axis because of the tilt.
Revolution: elliptical orbit in 365¼ days → leap year (366 days) every 4 years; perihelion ~Jan, aphelion ~Jul.
Summer solstice 21 Jun — Sun over Tropic of Cancer, longest NH day; winter solstice 22 Dec — Sun over Tropic of Capricorn.
Equinoxes 21 Mar & 23 Sep — Sun over the equator, equal day and night worldwide.
Poles experience about six months of daylight followed by six months of darkness.

items.title: Latitudes, Longitudes, Heat Zones & Time
items.body:
### Latitudes, Longitudes, Heat Zones and Time

**In one line**
Latitudes and longitudes are the grid of lines that pin down any place on Earth, set its heat zone, and — through longitude — tell its time.

**The story**
**Latitudes** are the east–west circles measured north and south of the **equator (0°)**, from 0° up to 90° at the poles; each degree is about **111 km** apart. A few of them matter most: the **Tropic of Cancer (23½°N)**, the **Tropic of Capricorn (23½°S)**, and the **Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66½°)**. They carve the Earth into three **heat zones**. **Longitudes** are the north–south lines running from pole to pole, measured east and west of the **Prime Meridian at Greenwich (0°)** up to 180°. Their special job is **time**: because the Earth turns a full 360° in 24 hours, it turns **15° every hour**, so **1° equals 4 minutes** of time. Places east of Greenwich see the Sun earlier, so their clocks are ahead.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The 1° ≈ 111 km fact, the heat-zone limits, the 15°-per-hour rule and the IST meridian are all exam staples.

**Picture it**

| Zone | Lies between |
|---|---|
| Torrid | Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn |
| Temperate | the tropics and the polar circles |
| Frigid | the polar circles and the poles |

**Terms explained**
- **Parallel** — another word for a latitude line.
- **Meridian** — another word for a longitude line.
- **Prime Meridian** — the 0° longitude line through Greenwich, the world's time reference; it divides the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
- **IST (Indian Standard Time)** — India's single clock time, set by the 82½°E meridian.

**Same meridian, same local time**
All places on the **same meridian** have the **same local (sun) time** — the Sun crosses the whole meridian at noon at once. Places east of a meridian are ahead in time; places west are behind.

**Don't confuse**
Latitude gives climate/heat zones; longitude gives time. The International Date Line roughly follows 180°, not the Prime Meridian.

**Remember it**
"Latitude = how hot (111 km a degree); Longitude = what time (4 minutes a degree)."

**TL;DR**
- Latitudes 0°–90° N/S of the equator; 1° ≈ 111 km; key lines at 23½° (tropics) and 66½° (polar circles).
- Heat zones: Torrid (between the tropics), Temperate, Frigid.
- Longitudes 0°–180° E/W of Greenwich; the Date Line is near 180°.
- Earth turns 15° per hour (1° = 4 minutes); India's 82½°E meridian makes IST = GMT + 5:30.
keyPoints: Latitudes run 0°–90° N/S from the equator; 1° of latitude ≈ 111 km.
Tropic of Cancer 23½°N, Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S, Arctic Circle 66½°N, Antarctic Circle 66½°S.
Heat zones: Torrid (between the tropics), Temperate (tropics to polar circles), Frigid (polar circles to poles).
Longitudes: 0°–180° E/W of the Prime Meridian (Greenwich); 360 meridians; IDL ≈ 180°.
Earth rotates 15° of longitude per hour (1° = 4 minutes); east of Greenwich is ahead in time.
India's standard meridian is 82½°E, so IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

items.title: Astronomy Basics — Eclipses, Seasons, Dwarf Planets & Time
items.body:
### Astronomy Essentials — Eclipses, Seasons, Dwarf Planets and Time

**In one line**
This note pulls together four high-yield points — why eclipses are rare, why the tilt (not distance) makes seasons, the five dwarf planets, and how to turn longitude into time.

**The story**
**Eclipses** need a straight line of Sun, Earth and Moon. A **solar** eclipse comes on a **new moon**, a **lunar** one on a **full moon**. They are not monthly because the Moon's orbit is tilted about **5°**, so most months the shadow misses; an eclipse happens only when a new or full moon falls near a **node**, where the two orbit planes cross. **Seasons** are caused by the Earth's **23½° tilt**, not by its distance from the Sun — the proof is that the Earth is actually **farthest** (aphelion) in early July, yet the Northern Hemisphere then has summer. The **dwarf planets** are worlds that are round and orbit the Sun but have not cleared their path. And **time** follows longitude: 15° per hour, 1° per 4 minutes.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
"Why not an eclipse every month", the tilt-not-distance logic, and simple longitude-to-time sums all appear regularly.

**Picture it**

| Point | Key fact |
|---|---|
| Solar eclipse | new moon, Moon between Sun and Earth |
| Lunar eclipse | full moon, Earth between Sun and Moon |
| Seasons | caused by the 23½° tilt, not distance |
| Dwarf planets | Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake |

**Umbra, penumbra, antumbra**
The Moon casts a dark inner shadow (the **umbra**) and a lighter outer one (the **penumbra**). During a total solar eclipse the observer stands **within the Moon's umbra**; in the penumbra the eclipse is only partial; beyond the umbra's tip (the antumbra) it is annular — the 'ring of fire'.

**Terms explained**
- **Ecliptic** — the flat plane of the Earth's orbit around the Sun.
- **Node** — a point where the Moon's tilted orbit crosses the ecliptic.
- **Aphelion / perihelion** — Earth's farthest (about 152 million km, early July) and nearest (about 147 million km, early January) points.

**Worked example — longitude into time**
At 82½°E (the IST meridian) a clock shows 10:00 AM. How late is it at Kohima (94°E)?
1. Longitude difference = 94° − 82½° = 11½°.
2. Each degree is 4 minutes of time, so 11½° × 4 = 46 minutes.
3. Kohima is east of 82½°E, so it is ahead: 10:00 AM + 46 min = **10:46 AM**.

**Why an annular eclipse shows a 'ring of fire'**
The Moon's orbit is oval. When a solar eclipse happens with the Moon near its **farthest point** from the Earth, the Moon looks **smaller than the Sun's disc**, so it cannot cover the Sun fully — a bright ring of sunlight is left uncovered. That is an **annular** eclipse (the observer is in the antumbra).

**Don't confuse**
Seasons are about tilt, not nearness to the Sun. Charon is Pluto's moon, not a dwarf planet.

**Remember it**
"Eclipses need a node; seasons need a tilt; time needs 4 minutes a degree."

**TL;DR**
- Solar eclipse on a new moon, lunar on a full moon; both need the Moon near a node (its orbit tilts about 5°).
- Seasons come from the 23½° axial tilt, not Earth–Sun distance (aphelion is in July).
- The IAU recognises five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake.
- 15° of longitude = 1 hour, 1° = 4 minutes; places east are ahead; IST = GMT + 5:30.
keyPoints: Solar eclipse on new moon (Moon between Sun and Earth); lunar eclipse on full moon (Earth between Sun and Moon).
Eclipses are not monthly because the Moon's orbit tilts ~5°; they need a new/full moon near a node.
Seasons are caused by the 23½° axial tilt, not the Earth–Sun distance.
Earth is at aphelion (~152 M km) in early July and perihelion (~147 M km) in early January.
IAU recognises five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake (Charon is a moon).
15° longitude = 1 hour, 1° = 4 minutes; places east of the reference meridian are ahead in time.
IST is based on 82½°E and is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
items.mnemonic: Solar = New moon (both start with the Sun's shadow on us); Lunar = fuLL moon.
items.source: International Astronomical Union (IAU); local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Motions of the Earth; Latitudes & Longitudes; Stars and The Solar System

items.title: High-yield Named Facts — Habitable Zone, Early Earth & Sky Navigation
items.body:
### High-Yield Named Facts — Habitable Zone, Early Earth and Sky Navigation

**In one line**
A cluster of named facts that sit around the core topic — the Goldilocks zone, the oxygen-free early Earth, magnetic reversals and the Pole Star — each a ready-made prelims answer.

**The story**
Scientists hunting for life-friendly worlds look at the **Goldilocks (habitable) zone** — the band around a star that is "just right", neither too hot nor too cold, so that **liquid water** can exist. On our own planet, the **early atmosphere** had almost **no free oxygen**; it was mostly carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour and nitrogen. Only later did tiny photosynthesising organisms slowly release **oxygen** (the Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago) — so life itself *reshaped* the air. The Earth's **magnetic field** also flips its north and south poles from time to time, a record frozen into the rocks of the sea floor. And for finding direction, the **Pole Star** sits almost over the north pole of the sky, so it hardly moves.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
These are lifted straight from UPSC/APPSC prelims (habitable zone, "life modified the atmosphere", geomagnetic reversal, Pole Star navigation).

**Picture it**

| Fact | Why it is asked |
|---|---|
| Goldilocks zone | search for Earth-like exoplanets (Kepler, TESS) |
| Early atmosphere | had no free oxygen; life added it |
| Magnetic reversal | recorded as stripes across mid-ocean ridges |
| Pole Star | marks true north for navigation |

**The Iron Catastrophe**
About 500 million years after the Earth formed, heat from radioactive decay plus leftover heat raised the young Earth to **iron's melting point** (about 1,538°C). The molten heavy metals — **iron and nickel — sank to the centre and formed the core**, while lighter silicate rock rose to form the mantle and crust. This sorting into layers is called **planetary differentiation**.

**What keeps the Earth's surface changing (UPSC 2013)**
All six of these drive dynamic change on the surface:
| Agent | How it changes the surface |
|---|---|
| Electromagnetic (solar) radiation | heats the surface, drives weathering, winds, rain and running water |
| Geothermal energy | inner heat that powers volcanoes, earthquakes and mountain building |
| Gravitational force | pulls rock and water downhill (landslides, rivers, glaciers) and raises tides |
| Plate movements | build mountains, open rifts and ocean basins |
| Rotation of the Earth | Coriolis deflection steers winds and ocean currents; daily heating and cooling |
| Revolution of the Earth | with the tilt, brings the seasons and their changing heat |

**Terms explained**
- **Habitable (Goldilocks) zone** — the orbit around a star where temperatures allow liquid water.
- **Great Oxidation Event** — the rise of free oxygen about 2.4 billion years ago from early photosynthesis.
- **Pointer stars** — Merak and Dubhe in Ursa Major (the Saptarishi / Great Bear) that point to the Pole Star.

**Don't confuse**
The early atmosphere was oxygen-poor, not oxygen-rich; oxygen came *after* life began. The Pole Star is not the brightest star (that is Sirius).

**Remember it**
"Goldilocks = liquid water; early air = no oxygen (life made it); Pole Star = true north via the Great Bear."

**TL;DR**
- Goldilocks/habitable zone: the orbit where liquid water can exist — used to shortlist exoplanets.
- Earth's early atmosphere had no free oxygen; photosynthesising life added it later.
- Earth's magnetic field reverses over time, recorded as paleomagnetic stripes on the sea floor.
- The Pole Star (Polaris) marks true north, found using the pointer stars of Ursa Major.
keyPoints: The Goldilocks/habitable zone is the orbit around a star where liquid water can exist — context: search for Earth-like exoplanets.
Earth's early atmosphere had no free oxygen; O₂ built up later from photosynthesis by early life (life modified the atmosphere).
Earth's magnetic field reverses polarity over geological time, recorded as paleomagnetic stripes across mid-ocean ridges.
Dynamic surface-change agents (UPSC 2013 — all six): solar electromagnetic radiation, geothermal energy, gravity, plate movements, Earth's rotation and revolution.
The Pole Star (Polaris) marks true north; it is located using the pointer stars of Ursa Major (Saptarishi).
items.source: UPSC CSE Prelims 2013/2015/2018; NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography; local APPSC GK PDF — Stars and the Solar System

items.title: Origin of the Universe & Solar System — Theories, Galaxies & Early Earth
items.body:
### How the universe, the solar system and the Earth began

**In one line**
The universe began with the **Big Bang** about **13.7 billion years** ago; our solar system condensed from a **solar nebula** about **4.6 billion years** ago; and the young Earth melted and sorted itself into layers.

**The story**
**Astronomy** is the study of celestial objects and is one of the oldest sciences — ancient Indians used it for calendars, festivals, sowing seasons and rainfall forecasts. **Celestial objects** are the natural bodies of the **Observable Universe** (the part we can see from Earth). In **1920** **Edwin Hubble** showed that galaxies are moving apart — the universe is **expanding**. Run the film backwards and everything started from one tiny point: the **Big Bang** (proposed by **Georges Lemaître**). A rival idea, the **Steady State** theory of **Fred Hoyle**, said the universe always looked the same; evidence now favours the Big Bang.

Our Sun is one star in the **Milky Way** galaxy (in India the **Akash Ganga**), a barred spiral. A **galaxy** is a huge system of stars, gas and dust held by gravity.

**Theories of the solar system's origin**

| Theory | Who | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| Nebular Hypothesis | **Immanuel Kant**, revised by **Laplace** (1796) | planets formed from a slowly rotating cloud (nebula) around the young Sun |
| Planetesimal Hypothesis | **Chamberlin and Moulton** (1900) | a wandering star passed near the Sun and pulled out material that became planets |
| Tidal / binary ideas | **Sir James Jeans**, later **Sir Harold Jeffreys** | supported the passing-star (tidal) idea |
| Revised nebular hypothesis | **Otto Schmidt** (Russia) and **Carl Weizsacker** (Germany), 1950 | Sun surrounded by a solar nebula of hydrogen, helium and dust; friction and collisions made a disc, then planets |

**How the Sun and planets formed (modern picture)**
- The nebula began to collapse some **5–5.6 billion years ago**, probably triggered by the shock waves of a nearby **supernova**.
- About **99.9%** of the matter fell to the centre; when it grew hot enough, **nuclear fusion** started and the Sun was born.
- The remaining **0.1%** flattened into a **protoplanetary disc**.
- Dust grains collided and stuck (**accretion**) into **planetesimals** a few km across, which grew into **proto-planets** and then planets.
- Rocks that escaped the planets' pull remained as **asteroids**, many in the **asteroid belt** between Mars and Jupiter.

**The young Earth — Iron Catastrophe and differentiation**
The Earth formed about **4.5–4.54 billion years ago** as a uniform ball of hot rock. Radioactive decay and leftover heat raised it, after about **500 million years**, to the melting point of iron (about **1,538°C**) — the **Iron Catastrophe**. Heavy **iron and nickel** sank to form the core while light silicates, water and air stayed outside: **planetary differentiation**.

**Terms explained**
- **Supernova** — the explosive death of a massive star.
- **Planetesimal** — a small body (up to a few km) built by accretion.

**Don't confuse**
Kant–Laplace = nebular (a cloud); Chamberlin–Moulton = planetesimal (a passing star). Hubble showed expansion; Lemaître proposed the Big Bang.

**TL;DR**
- Big Bang ~13.7 billion years ago; Hubble (1920) showed the universe is expanding; Steady State theory = Fred Hoyle.
- Nebular Hypothesis: Kant, revised by Laplace (1796); Planetesimal: Chamberlin and Moulton (1900); revised nebular: Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizsacker.
- Nebula collapse 5–5.6 billion years ago (supernova trigger); 99.9% to the Sun, 0.1% to the protoplanetary disc.
- Iron Catastrophe at ~1,538°C about 500 million years after formation → planetary differentiation.
keyPoints: Big Bang about 13.7 billion years ago; Edwin Hubble (1920) proved the universe is expanding; Georges Lemaître proposed the Big Bang.
Steady State theory — Fred Hoyle.
Nebular Hypothesis — Immanuel Kant, revised by Laplace (1796); Planetesimal Hypothesis — Chamberlin and Moulton (1900).
Revised nebular hypothesis — Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizsacker (1950).
Milky Way (Akash Ganga) is our galaxy; it is a barred spiral.
Only 0.1% of nebular matter stayed in orbit as the protoplanetary disc; accretion built planetesimals → proto-planets → planets.

items.title: The Sun — Size, Layers, Solar Activity & Life Cycle
items.body:
### Inside the Sun and its storms

**In one line**
The Sun is a middle-aged star, **109 times** wider than Earth, built in layers from a fusion **core** to the **corona**, and its surface throws out sunspots, flares, prominences and the solar wind.

**The story**
The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system and the primary source of light and heat. Its diameter is about **1.4 million km**, roughly **109 times** that of Earth. It shines because hydrogen fuses into helium in its core. Energy then travels outward in stages — by radiation, then by convection — until it escapes from the visible surface. The Sun is about **5 billion years old**, in the **middle** of its life, and will shine for about **5 billion more** years. Then it will swell into a **red giant** (perhaps engulfing Mercury, Venus and Earth), shed its outer layers and leave a **white dwarf**.

**Layers from inside out**

| Layer | What happens |
|---|---|
| Core | nuclear fusion produces energy (about 15 million °C) |
| Radiative zone | energy moves outward by radiation |
| Convective zone | energy moves by convection — hot gas rises, cool gas sinks |
| Photosphere | the visible surface that emits light (about 5,500°C) |
| Chromosphere | above the photosphere; seen as a **red ring** during a solar eclipse |
| Corona | outermost layer; a halo of light seen during a **total** solar eclipse |

**Solar activity**

| Feature | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Sunspots | dark patches **500–1,500°C cooler** than their surroundings; last days to months; the Sun is about **1% cooler** during sunspot activity |
| Solar wind | stream of charged particles (electrons, protons) at up to **900 km/s**, about **1 million °C**; interacts with Earth's magnetic field (auroras) |
| Solar flares | bursts of energy from magnetic anomalies; heat the corona to **10–20 million °C** |
| Solar prominences | huge arcs of gas held by magnetic fields; many erupt into space |

**India's Sun mission**
**Aditya-L1** (launched **2 September 2023** from **Sriharikota**, Andhra Pradesh) studies the Sun from the **Lagrange point L1**, about **1.5 million km** from Earth.

**Terms explained**
- **Lagrange point** — a spot where the pulls of the Sun and Earth balance, so a craft can "park".

**Don't confuse**
Chromosphere = red ring; corona = outer halo (and gets *hotter* than the surface). Sunspots are cooler, not hotter.

**TL;DR**
- Diameter ~1.4 million km (109 × Earth); about 5 billion years old, 5 billion more to go; red giant → white dwarf.
- Layers: core → radiative zone → convective zone → photosphere → chromosphere → corona.
- Sunspots 500–1,500°C cooler; solar wind up to 900 km/s; flares heat the corona to 10–20 million °C.
- Aditya-L1 observes the Sun from L1 (~1.5 million km), launched from Sriharikota.
keyPoints: Sun diameter about 1.4 million km — about 109 times Earth.
Layers: core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere (visible surface), chromosphere (red ring), corona (halo in total eclipse).
Sunspots are 500–1,500°C cooler; solar wind up to 900 km/s at about 1 million °C.
Solar flares heat the corona to 10–20 million °C; solar prominences are magnetic arcs of gas.
Sun is ~5 billion years old, mid-life; will become a red giant then a white dwarf.
Aditya-L1 (2 September 2023, Sriharikota) studies the Sun from Lagrange point L1, ~1.5 million km away.

items.title: The Eight Planets — Data Table & Superlatives
items.body:
### Planet-by-planet data

**In one line**
One table holds almost every planet number examiners use — and a short list of "est" facts (densest, fastest, most moons) answers most single-fact questions.

**The story**
Going outward from the Sun the order is **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**. A **planet** is a body moving in an **elliptical orbit** around a star. Distances are often given in **Astronomical Units** (1 AU = average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km).

| Planet (Indian name) | Rotation | Revolution | Distance (AU) | Diameter (km) | Moons* | Density (g/cm³) | Spin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury (Budh) | 58.6 days | 88 days | 0.39 | 4,880 | 0 | 5.43 | W→E |
| Venus (Shukra) | 243 days | 225 days | 0.72 | 12,104 | 0 | 5.24 | E→W |
| Earth (Prithvi) | 24 hours | 365.25 days | 1 | 12,742 | 1 | 5.51 | W→E |
| Mars (Mangal) | 24.6 hours | 687 days | 1.52 | 6,779 | 2 | 3.93 | W→E |
| Jupiter (Brihaspati) | 9.9 hours | 11.86 years | 5.2 | 139,820 | 95 | 1.33 | W→E |
| Saturn (Shani) | 10.7 hours | 29.46 years | 9.58 | 116,460 | 82* | 0.69 | W→E |
| Uranus (Arun) | 17.2 hours | 84 years | 19.18 | 50,724 | 27 | 1.27 | E→W |
| Neptune (Varun) | 16.1 hours | 164.8 years | 30.07 | 49,244 | 14 | 1.64 | W→E |

*Moon counts keep changing. Our source table gives Jupiter 95 and Saturn 82; with new discoveries confirmed in 2023–2025, **Saturn now has the most moons (274 recognised in 2025)**.

**Superlatives**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Densest planet | **Earth** (5.51) |
| Least dense (would float on water) | **Saturn** (0.69) |
| Shortest year / fastest orbit | **Mercury** (88 days) |
| Fastest spin (shortest day) | **Jupiter** (9.9 hours) — so it is an **oblate spheroid** |
| Slowest spin (longest day) | **Venus** (243 days) |
| Longest year | **Neptune** (164.8 years) |
| No moons | **Mercury and Venus** |
| Retrograde (east-to-west, clockwise) spin | **Venus and Uranus** |

**Planet notes**
- **Mercury** — almost no atmosphere, so the widest day–night range (about **427°C by day to −173°C at night**). It is **smaller than Ganymede and Titan** but has **more mass** than both.
- **Venus** — **brightest planet** and third-brightest object after the Sun and Moon; **highest albedo** from reflective **sulphuric acid** clouds; atmosphere about **96% carbon dioxide**; surface pressure **92 times** Earth's; called **Earth's twin** (similar size, mass, composition); seen as the **morning and evening star**.
- **Mars** — red from **iron oxide**; thin air (pressure under **1%** of Earth's), so no surface liquid water though landforms show water once flowed; lost its **magnetosphere about 4 billion years ago**; air about **96% CO₂, 1.93% argon, 1.89% nitrogen**; **methane** detected; moons **Phobos and Deimos**; **Olympus Mons**, the highest volcano in the solar system.
- **Jupiter** — no solid surface; banded atmosphere and the **Great Red Spot** storm; four **Galilean moons** found by Galileo: **Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto** — Ganymede (**5,268 km**) is the largest moon of all.
- **Saturn** — rings of billions of ice particles and ice-covered rocks; moon **Titan**.
- **Uranus and Neptune** — the **ice giants**, "twins of the outer solar system", rich in water, ammonia and methane ices.

**Terms explained**
- **Albedo** — the share of sunlight a surface reflects.
- **Oblate spheroid** — a sphere bulging at the equator.

**Don't confuse**
Mercury is closest but **Venus** is hottest. Jupiter is biggest, but **Saturn** has the most moons (current count).

**TL;DR**
- Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
- Earth densest; Saturn least dense; Mercury fastest orbit (88 days); Jupiter fastest spin (9.9 h); Venus slowest spin (243 days).
- Mercury and Venus have no moons; Mars has Phobos and Deimos; Saturn has the most moons.
- Venus: brightest, highest albedo, 96% CO₂, 92× pressure; Mars: iron oxide, Olympus Mons.
keyPoints: Planet order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Earth is the densest planet; Saturn the least dense (would float).
Mercury: 88-day year; Jupiter: 9.9-hour day; Venus: 243-day day; Neptune: 164.8-year year; Uranus: 84 years.
Mercury and Venus have no moons; Mars has Phobos and Deimos; Saturn now has the most moons.
Venus is the brightest planet with the highest albedo (sulphuric acid clouds), 96% CO2 and 92 times Earth pressure; morning and evening star.
Mars: iron oxide, Olympus Mons, pressure under 1%, lost magnetosphere about 4 billion years ago, methane detected.
Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto; Jupiter has the Great Red Spot.

items.title: Dwarf Planets, Asteroids, Comets & Meteors — Definitions & Numbers
items.body:
### The small bodies and the IAU rules

**In one line**
The **IAU (2006)** fixed what a planet is; bodies that fail only the "cleared its orbit" test are dwarf planets, and the rest — asteroids, comets, meteoroids — are small Solar System bodies.

**The story**
In **2006** the **International Astronomical Union**, meeting at **Prague**, voted on a definition of a planet, and **Pluto** was demoted to a **dwarf planet**. Pluto (diameter **2,377 km**) shares the **Kuiper Belt** with many similar icy bodies, such as **Eris** (**2,326 km**), so it cannot have cleared its neighbourhood.

**IAU definition of a planet — all four must be true**
1. It **orbits the Sun**.
2. It has enough mass to reach **hydrostatic equilibrium** (a nearly round shape).
3. It is **not a satellite** of another object.
4. It has **cleared** debris and small objects from around its orbit.

A **dwarf planet** meets 1–3 but **not 4**.

**Asteroids, Ceres and the belts**

| Body / region | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Asteroid belt | remnant of planet formation between **Mars and Jupiter** that failed to form a planet because of **Jupiter's gravitational interference** |
| Asteroids | made of refractory **rocky and metallic** minerals; from hundreds of km to microscopic; all except Ceres are "small Solar System bodies" |
| Ceres | largest asteroid (**946 km**), a proto-planet and a **dwarf planet** — round under its own gravity |
| Kuiper Belt | like the asteroid belt but far larger, from Neptune's orbit at **30 AU to 50 AU**; may be treated as the **extent of the Solar System** (the Sun's pull matches that of other stars) |
| Oort Cloud | far-distant shell of icy bodies, source of long-period comets |

**Comets**
A **comet** is an icy small body. Near the Sun, solar radiation and the solar wind heat its **nucleus**, which **outgasses** to form a glowing **coma** and often a **tail** — the tail always points **away from the Sun**. Comets have **highly elliptical** orbits (planets' orbits are near-circular). **Halley's Comet** returns about every **76 years**; it last came in **1986** and is next due in **2061**.

**Meteoroid → meteor → meteorite**
Colliding asteroids chip off small pieces — **meteoroids**. One that enters the atmosphere heats by **friction** and shows as a streak of light, a **meteor** or "**shooting star**" (it is rock, not a star); most burn up. Any piece reaching the ground is a **meteorite**. When Earth passes through a **comet's tail/debris**, many meteors appear — a **meteor shower**.

**Don't confuse**
Asteroids are rocky/metallic and lie mostly between Mars and Jupiter; comets are icy and show tails. Ceres is in the asteroid belt; Pluto and Eris in the Kuiper Belt.

**TL;DR**
- IAU 2006 (Prague): orbit the Sun, round, not a satellite, cleared orbit; Pluto became a dwarf planet.
- Pluto 2,377 km, Eris 2,326 km (Kuiper Belt); Ceres 946 km (asteroid belt).
- Asteroid belt exists because of Jupiter's gravity; Kuiper Belt 30–50 AU.
- Comet tail points away from the Sun; Halley's Comet every 76 years (1986, next 2061); meteor shower = Earth crosses comet debris.
keyPoints: IAU (2006, Prague) planet test: orbits the Sun, hydrostatic equilibrium (round), not a satellite, cleared its orbit.
Pluto (2,377 km) was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006; Eris is 2,326 km.
Ceres (946 km) is the largest asteroid and a dwarf planet.
The asteroid belt failed to form a planet because of Jupiter's gravitational interference.
Kuiper Belt: 30 AU to 50 AU — may be taken as the extent of the Solar System.
A comet's coma and tail form by outgassing near the Sun; the tail points away from the Sun.
Halley's Comet returns every 76 years — last 1986, next 2061.
Meteor shower: Earth passes through a comet's tail; meteors are called shooting stars.

items.title: The Moon — Phases, Festivals, Surface, Origin & Missions
items.body:
### Our Moon in detail

**In one line**
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, shining by reflected sunlight through **eight phases**, born of a **giant impact** about **4.44 billion years** ago, and visited by Apollo 11 and Chandrayaan-3.

**The story**
As the Moon circles the Earth, the half facing the Sun is lit. We see different amounts of that lit half — the **phases** — which repeat about every **29 days** (29.5 days, the synodic month) in **eight major phases**. On **Full Moon** day the whole face is lit; about 15 days later the Moon lies on the Sun's side and is invisible — **New Moon**. The next night a thin **Crescent** appears. Growing is **waxing**; shrinking is **waning**. When a calendar month has **two full moons**, the second is a **Blue Moon**.

The Moon is about **384,400 km** away, **3,474 km** across (the **fifth-largest** moon) and takes about **27.3 days** to orbit (sidereal month). It spins once per orbit, so we always see the **same face**.

**Phases and Indian festivals**

| Festival | Moon phase |
|---|---|
| Diwali | New Moon day (Amavasya) |
| Guru Nanak Jayanti | Full Moon day |
| Maha Shivratri | the 13th/14th night of the waning moon |
| Eid-ul-Fitr | the day after the crescent moon is sighted |

**Surface**
Barren and dusty; bowl-shaped **craters**; many steep, high mountains — some as high as Earth's highest. There is **no atmosphere** and no liquid water. (Our source says "no water"; India's **Chandrayaan-1** (2008) later detected water molecules/ice — so "no liquid water, but traces of water ice" is the safer answer.)

**Origin — the giant impact ("big splat")**
Shortly after Earth formed, a body **one to three times the size of Mars** (often named **Theia**) struck it, blasting material into orbit that gathered into the Moon about **4.44 billion years ago**.

**Missions**

| Mission | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Apollo 11 (USA) | **Neil Armstrong** first stepped on the Moon on **21 July 1969** (IST; 20 July in the USA), followed by **Edwin (Buzz) Aldrin** |
| Chandrayaan-3 (India) | third lunar mission, second soft-landing attempt; launched **14 July 2023** from **Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota** (Andhra Pradesh); lunar orbit **5 August 2023**; landed near the **lunar south pole** on **23 August 2023** |

**Don't confuse**
Sidereal month 27.3 days (one orbit) vs synodic month 29.5 days (phase cycle). Waxing = growing, waning = shrinking.

**TL;DR**
- 8 phases every ~29 days; waxing grows, waning shrinks; Blue Moon = second full moon in a month.
- Diwali — New Moon; Guru Nanak Jayanti — Full Moon; Eid-ul-Fitr — after the crescent.
- Distance 384,400 km; diameter 3,474 km (5th-largest moon); same face always seen.
- Giant impact by a Mars-sized body → Moon 4.44 billion years ago; Armstrong & Aldrin 1969; Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole 23 August 2023.
keyPoints: Eight major phases repeating about every 29 days; waxing = increasing, waning = decreasing.
Blue Moon = the second full moon in one calendar month.
Diwali on New Moon; Guru Nanak Jayanti on Full Moon; Maha Shivratri on the waning moon night; Eid-ul-Fitr after the crescent.
Moon: about 384,400 km away, 3,474 km wide (fifth-largest moon), always shows the same face.
Giant impact by a body 1–3 times the size of Mars formed the Moon about 4.44 billion years ago.
Neil Armstrong (then Edwin Aldrin) landed on 21 July 1969 (Apollo 11).
Chandrayaan-3: launched 14 July 2023 from Sriharikota, lunar orbit 5 August, landed near the lunar south pole 23 August 2023.

items.title: Types of Eclipses, Stars & Constellations
items.body:
### Eclipse types, stars and the night sky

**In one line**
There are three kinds of lunar eclipse and three kinds of solar eclipse; and a handful of stars and constellations — Ursa Major, Orion, Sirius, Cassiopeia, the Pole Star — are what exams ask about the night sky.

**The story**
A **lunar eclipse** (Earth between Sun and Moon, only at **Full Moon**) is visible from **anywhere on the night side** of the Earth. A **solar eclipse** (Moon between Earth and Sun, only at **New Moon**) is seen only where the Moon's small shadow falls.

**Lunar eclipses**

| Type | What happens |
|---|---|
| Total | the whole Moon enters Earth's **umbra**; it often turns red — a "**blood moon**" — because Earth's atmosphere scatters and bends sunlight onto it |
| Partial | only part of the Moon enters the umbra |
| Penumbral | the Moon passes only through the **penumbra**; faint, hard to notice |

**Solar eclipses**

| Type | What happens |
|---|---|
| Total | Moon covers the Sun completely; the **corona** becomes visible |
| Partial | only part of the Sun is covered |
| Annular | Moon is farther away, looks smaller, leaves a "**ring of fire**" (antumbra) |

The **Saros cycle** — about **18 years, 11 days and 8 hours** — is the interval after which eclipses repeat almost identically.

**Stars**
**Stars** are huge balls of hot gas, mainly **hydrogen and helium**, that **emit their own light**; they differ in brightness, size, colour and temperature, and look like points only because they are so far away. They are born, live for millions of years and die, changing so slowly that they seem permanent. The nearest star to Earth is the **Sun**; the next is **Proxima Centauri** (about **4.24 light-years**). A **light-year** (about **9.46 trillion km**) is a distance, not a time.

**Constellations** — groups of stars forming a recognisable pattern, used by ancient people for navigation. Stars in one constellation only *look* close; they may be at very different distances.

| Constellation / star | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Ursa Major (Great Bear, **Saptarishi**, Big Dipper) | **seven** main stars like a ladle/question mark — **3 in the handle, 4 in the bowl**; in Indian tradition seven sages preserving the Vedas |
| Pointer stars | **Merak and Dubhe** in Ursa Major — the line through them leads to the **Pole Star** |
| Pole Star (Polaris, Dhruva) | sits near Earth's axis of rotation, so its position stays fixed — marks north |
| Orion (the Hunter) | 7–8 bright stars; a **belt of 3 stars** with 4 stars in a quadrilateral |
| Sirius | the **brightest star** in the night sky; a line through **Orion's belt** points to it. (Our source places Sirius "in Orion"; standard references put it in **Canis Major**, the Great Dog — Orion only points to it.) |
| Cassiopeia | Northern Hemisphere, seen in winter, shaped like a **W** (or distorted M); named after a Greek queen |
| Leo Major | seen from both hemispheres (upside down in the south); recognised ~6,000 years ago; linked to Hercules |

**Don't confuse**
Brightest star = Sirius; the Pole Star is not the brightest. Penumbral lunar eclipse ≠ annular solar eclipse.

**TL;DR**
- Lunar: total (blood moon), partial, penumbral; visible from the whole night side.
- Solar: total (corona visible), partial, annular (ring of fire).
- Saros cycle = 18 years 11 days 8 hours.
- Ursa Major: 7 stars, Merak and Dubhe point to Polaris; Orion's belt of 3 stars points to Sirius (in Canis Major); Cassiopeia is W-shaped.
keyPoints: Lunar eclipse types: total (blood moon), partial, penumbral; visible from the whole night side of Earth.
Solar eclipse types: total (corona visible), partial, annular (ring of fire).
Saros cycle: about 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours.
Stars are mainly hydrogen and helium and emit their own light; Proxima Centauri is ~4.24 light-years away.
Ursa Major (Saptarishi): 7 stars — 3 handle, 4 bowl; pointer stars Merak and Dubhe lead to the Pole Star.
Orion's belt of 3 stars points to Sirius, the brightest star (in Canis Major).
Cassiopeia is W-shaped and seen in northern winter.

items.title: Rotation & Revolution — Numbers, Solstice vs Equinox, Day Length
items.body:
### The motions in numbers

**In one line**
Rotation gives day and night; revolution on a **tilted axis** gives the seasons and the changing length of day — and a few numbers and Latin roots finish the topic.

**The story**
The Earth's shape is a **geoid** — slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator (equatorial diameter about **12,756 km**, polar about **12,714 km**). It spins on an imaginary axis through the poles, **west to east**. Measured against the Sun, one turn takes **24 hours** (a **solar day**); measured against the distant stars it takes **23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds** (a **sidereal day**). A point on the equator moves at about **1,670 km/h**.

It also **revolves** around the Sun on an elliptical orbit in **365¼ days**, at about **30 km per second**. The extra quarter day becomes **29 February** every fourth year (a **leap year**, 366 days); century years are leap years only if divisible by **400** (2000 was, 1900 was not).

**Why do day and night lengths change through the year?**
Because the Earth **revolves round the Sun on a tilted axis** (UPSC 2013). If the axis were upright, every place would get 12 hours of day all year. The **circle of illumination** (the day–night line) does not pass through the poles because of the tilt. Only at the **equator** is day always about **12 hours**. Twilight is shortest at the equator and longest at the poles.

**Solstice vs equinox**

| | Equinox | Solstice |
|---|---|---|
| Dates | 21 March and 23 September | 21 June and 22 December |
| Sun overhead (subsolar point) | Equator (Sun at 90° to the equator) | 23½°N (June) or 23½°S (December) |
| Day/night | equal everywhere | longest/shortest of the year |
| Season | start of spring or autumn | midsummer or midwinter |
| Latin root | **aequi** (equal) + **noctium** (night) | **sol** (sun) + **stitium** (standing still) |

The **21 March** equinox is the **vernal (spring) equinox** and **23 September** the **autumnal equinox** in the Northern Hemisphere — the seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere.

**Polar days**
On **21 June** the Arctic Circle gets 24 hours of daylight; on **22 December** the **Antarctic Circle** does. The poles get about **six months of day and six months of night**.

**Perihelion and aphelion**
Earth is nearest the Sun (**perihelion**, ~147 million km) about **3 January** and farthest (**aphelion**, ~152 million km) about **4 July**.

**Don't confuse**
Sidereal day 23 h 56 min (stars) vs solar day 24 h (Sun). Equinox = equal night; solstice = sun standing still.

**TL;DR**
- Geoid shape; equatorial diameter ~12,756 km vs polar ~12,714 km.
- Sidereal day 23 h 56 min 4 s; solar day 24 h; equator spins at ~1,670 km/h; orbit speed ~30 km/s.
- Leap year: 29 February; century years only if divisible by 400.
- Day-length changes come from revolution on a tilted axis; perihelion ~3 January, aphelion ~4 July.
keyPoints: Earth is a geoid — equatorial diameter about 12,756 km, polar about 12,714 km.
Sidereal day = 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds; solar day = 24 hours.
Equatorial rotation speed about 1,670 km/h; orbital speed about 30 km per second.
Leap year adds 29 February; a century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400.
Seasonal changes in day length are due to revolution on a tilted axis; the equator always has about 12 hours of day.
Equinox from aequi + noctium (equal night); solstice from sol + stitium (sun standing still).
Vernal equinox 21 March, autumnal equinox 23 September (Northern Hemisphere).
Perihelion about 3 January (~147 million km); aphelion about 4 July (~152 million km).

items.title: Latitude vs Longitude, Date Line, Time Zones & the India/AP Angle
items.body:
### The global grid and time — details

**In one line**
Latitudes are 179 parallel circles (φ) that set heat zones; longitudes are 360 half-circle meridians (λ) that set time; the Date Line, time zones and India's single standard time follow from this.

**The story**
**Parallels of latitude** get smaller away from the equator; including the equator there are **179** of them (181 if the poles were counted as lines — they are points). A degree of latitude is about **110.6 km at the equator and 111.7 km at the poles** (because the Earth is flattened). **Meridians of longitude** are **semicircles** joining the poles; the gap between them shrinks towards the poles and becomes **zero** at the poles. There are **360** meridians — 180° east and 180° west of the **Prime Meridian** through **Greenwich** (fixed at the **International Meridian Conference, 1884**). Where a parallel and a meridian cross gives the location of a place.

| Term | Latitude | Longitude |
|---|---|---|
| Symbol | Greek **phi (φ)** | Greek **lambda (λ)** |
| Range | 0°–90° N and S | 0°–180° E and W |
| Parallel? | yes | no — converge at the poles |
| Divides | Northern/Southern Hemispheres | Eastern/Western Hemispheres |
| Measured from | Equator | Prime Meridian |
| Number of lines | 179 | 360 |
| Notable lines | Equator, Tropics | Prime Meridian, International Date Line |
| Used for | temperature (heat) zones | time zones |

**International Date Line (IDL)**
Roughly along **180°**, exactly 12 hours from Greenwich whichever way you go. It **zigzags** to avoid splitting land and island groups. Crossing it **westward** (America → Asia) you **gain** a day (the date jumps forward); crossing **eastward** you **repeat** a day.

**Time zones**
The world has **24 time zones** of one hour, each about **15°** wide. Wide countries use several: **Russia has 11**; **France holds the record with 12** (counting overseas territories).

**India's standard time**
India's local times differ — **Dwarka (Gujarat)** and **Dibrugarh (Assam)** differ by about **1 hour 45 minutes** (India spans about **68°7'E to 97°25'E**, ~30° of longitude, i.e. about 2 hours). So India uses one **Indian Standard Time** based on **82°30'E**, which passes near **Mirzapur** (Uttar Pradesh). IST is **5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT**: when it is 2:00 pm in London, it is **7:30 pm** in India. The 82°30'E meridian passes through **five states — Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh** (near Kakinada/Yanam).

**The AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh lies about **12°37'N–19°54'N** and **76°46'E–84°46'E** — wholly in the Torrid Zone, south of the **Tropic of Cancer**. The Tropic of Cancer crosses **eight** Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram — not AP.

**Don't confuse**
Westward across the IDL = add a day; eastward = subtract. IST meridian passes through AP; the Tropic of Cancer does not.

**TL;DR**
- Latitude φ, 179 parallels, 1° = 110.6 km (equator) to 111.7 km (poles); longitude λ, 360 meridians, gap zero at poles.
- Prime Meridian at Greenwich (1884); IDL ~180°, zigzags; westward crossing gains a day.
- 24 time zones of 15°; Russia 11, France 12.
- IST 82°30'E (Mirzapur), GMT + 5:30; crosses UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh; Dwarka–Dibrugarh ~1 h 45 min.
keyPoints: Latitude is denoted phi (φ), longitude lambda (λ); 179 parallels and 360 meridians.
1° of latitude: 110.6 km at the equator, 111.7 km at the poles; meridian spacing becomes zero at the poles.
Prime Meridian through Greenwich, fixed at the International Meridian Conference of 1884.
International Date Line ~180°; zigzags around land; crossing westward gains a day.
24 time zones of 15° each; Russia has 11, France holds the record with 12.
Dwarka–Dibrugarh local time differs by about 1 hour 45 minutes; India spans about 68°7′E–97°25′E.
IST meridian 82°30′E passes near Mirzapur and through UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh; London 2 pm = India 7:30 pm.
Tropic of Cancer crosses eight states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram.

items.title: For Mains — Earth in the Solar System & Its Motions
items.body:
### For Mains — Earth, Its Motions and Time

**In one line**
For Mains (Paper-II General Studies, geography clause nearest M2-11), earth-and-motions is asked not as astronomy trivia but as the physical basis of climate, timekeeping and the monsoon, applied to India and Andhra Pradesh.

**The dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Rotation | day and night, the Coriolis effect that steers winds and cyclones, and local time. |
| Revolution + tilt | the march of seasons, varying day length, solstices and equinoxes. |
| Latitude | heat-zone and climate control; India straddling the Tropic of Cancer. |
| Longitude | the logic of a single standard time for a wide country. |
| Application | links to monsoon onset/retreat, agriculture and disaster timing. |
| Limits | why one standard meridian causes an east–west sunrise lag. |

**Data points to quote**
- Axial tilt 23½° (axis at 66½° to the orbital plane) is the cause of seasons, not Earth–Sun distance (aphelion is in July).
- 1° of longitude = 4 minutes of time; India (~68°E–97°E) spans about two hours of local time, yet uses one IST at 82½°E (GMT + 5:30).
- 1° of latitude ≈ 111 km; the Tropic of Cancer (23½°N) bisects India.
- Coriolis deflection: right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern (Ferrel's Law).

**The AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh (about 12.6°N–19.9°N) lies wholly in the tropics, just south of the Tropic of Cancer, giving it a warm climate year-round and a small seasonal temperature range; the revolution-driven shift of the overhead sun underlies its south-west and north-east monsoon seasons. Lying close to the 82½°E standard meridian, AP's clock time nearly matches its true solar time.

**Use in answers**
- Open by separating the two motions: rotation gives the day, revolution plus tilt gives the year of seasons.
- Use the "aphelion in July" fact to disprove the distance theory of seasons.
- Draw a simple tilted-Earth-and-Sun diagram marking the solstices and equinoxes.
- Close with the India/AP application — one standard time, tropical location and the monsoon.
keyPoints: Treat earth-and-motions analytically: the physical basis of climate, time and the monsoon, not astronomy trivia.
Seasons come from the 23½° tilt, not Earth–Sun distance (aphelion in July proves it).
1° longitude = 4 minutes; India spans ~2 hours yet uses one IST at 82½°E (GMT + 5:30).
AP angle: tropical location (~12.6°–19.9°N) → warm year-round, monsoon-driven seasons; near the 82½°E meridian.
Coriolis effect (Ferrel's Law) steers winds and cyclones; latitude controls heat zones.
